title: 19. How does cattle grazing of corn residues affect soil health in the long term?.
content:
Abstract
Corn residue grazing is widely practiced in beef production systems in the western corn belt; however, most studies evaluating its impacts on soil health have been short term ( < 5 yr) and report minimal effects. The objective of this study was to evaluate the long-term effects of grazing corn residue on soil health in an irrigated corn–soybean rotation. The study was conducted from 1997 to 2024 (26 yr) using a complete block design with four replications of grazed and non-grazed areas managed under no-till. Grazing occurred only on corn residue and therefore every other year (13 grazing years). Soils were predominantly Mollisols. Corn grain yields ranged from 12.5 to 15.0 Mg/ha (200 to 250 bu/ac) across years, with typical stocking rates ranging from 4.5 to 6.5 AUM/ha. Fifteen soil health indicators were evaluated at 0–5 and 5–10 cm depths. Data were analyzed using ANOVA with PROC GLIMMIX in SAS; significance was declared at P ≤ 0.05 and tendencies at 0.05 < P ≤ 0.10. Compared with non-grazed areas, grazed treatments tended to have greater bulk density at 0–5 cm (P = 0.06; 1.04 vs. 0.99 g/cm³), with no difference observed at 5–10 cm (P = 0.12). Bulk density values remained below thresholds associated with restricted root growth. Soil organic matter was lower (P = 0.02) in grazed areas at 0–5 cm (4.8 vs. 5.3%) but greater (P = 0.02) at 5–10 cm (4.0 vs. 3.8%) compared with non-grazed areas. At both depths, cation exchange capacity was greater (P ≤ 0.04) in grazed than non-grazed treatments (0–5 cm: 21.0 vs. 17.2; 5–10 cm: 22.7 vs. 19.0 meq/100 g), though values remained within the same soil fertility class. Earthworm abundance was greater (P = 0.03) in grazed compared with non-grazed areas (102 vs. 69 earthworms/m³), with a tendency (P = 0.08) for increased earthworm biomass (61.3 vs 42.2 g/m3). No differences (P ≥ 0.10) were observed between treatments for soil N, P, or K concentrations or cumulative water infiltration. Grazing corn residue resulted in measurable but limited changes to select soil health indicators, including modest shifts in bulk density, soil organic matter distribution, cation exchange capacity, and earthworm abundance. Importantly, these changes did not translate into biologically meaningful constraints to soil function, nutrient availability, or water infiltration. These findings demonstrate that long-term grazing of corn residue allows producers to capture value from corn residue without compromising soil health.
